capture.final_message:
Split the conjunction.

- For the first part, characterize lower semicontinuity using strict lower rays: if \(c<f(x)\), then \(f(x)\in(c,\infty)\). This ray is open in the order topology, so `ContinuousWithinAt f s x` makes \(f(z)>c\) eventually within \(s\).

- For the second part, use the standard stability of upper semicontinuity under addition. Given \(f(x)+g(x)<c\), continuity and monotonicity of addition provide compatible one-sided neighborhoods of \(f(x)\) and \(g(x)\) whose pairwise sums lie below \(c\). The two upper-semicontinuity hypotheses eventually place \(f(z)\) and \(g(z)\) in those neighborhoods; intersecting these eventual conditions yields \(f(z)+g(z)<c\).

Thus the proof should be organized by constructing the conjunction and applying the existing lemmas “continuous implies lower semicontinuous” and “the sum of two upper-semicontinuous functions is upper semicontinuous.” The essential assumption in the second part is continuity of addition; the ordered-additive structure supplies its monotonicity.
